text.p: The pound bounced back against the mark and the dollar, boosted by short-covering after Wednesday's sharp losses, traders said.
Sterling seesawed through the European session from an early peak at 2.7975 marks to a low of 2.7800 and back above 2.79 again.
It also recovered above $1.62 against the dollar after falling to its lowest level in nearly a month at $1.6154.

"This sort of volatility is quite common for the pound now," said Robert Hayward, economist at Bank of America. "It's subject to frequent bouts of profit-taking, followed by quite substantial buying at the lows."

Sterling slumped on Wednesday amid U.S. selling after an opinion poll in the Guardian newspaper showed a sharp decline in the opposition Labour party's lead, which prompted fears of a hung parliament. A CBI survey on Wednesday showing strong sterling is having a negative impact on exporters also weighed on the pound.

Markets would be susceptible to selling if the May 1 election resulted in a hung parliament because neither Labour nor the Conservatives would have enough votes to enact their legislative agenda and carry out clear-cut economic policy.

A MORI poll published in the Times today showed the Labour party still on course for victory, putting Labour at 48 percent, down one point over the past week, while the ruling Conservatives lost five points to 27 percent.
UK trade data confirmed that the strong pound hurt exports, but the pound took little notice since the figures were at the lower end of market expectations.
Britain's global trade deficit widened to 758 million stg in February from a revised 535 million in January but was less than the 813 million stg average forecast.
"There wasn't anything dramatic in the trade data, so the pound has been given a bit of support by the data," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
Ex-oil and erratics, the trade gap widened to 1.34 billion stg in February from 1.19 in January.
The non-EU trade gap totalled 606 million stg in March after a revised 437 million stg deficit in February and a touch less than the 613 million average forecast.

The prospect of a further deterioration in the trade balance was ultimately negative for the pound but positive interest rate differentials were likely to keep buoying sterling/mark, said Stamenkovic.

Another reminder about how the strong pound hits industry came from Britain's largest chemical company ICI. ICI said sterling's strength could reduce full-year profit by about 120 million sterling if it remained at current levels and attributed a large chunk of its 68 percent slump in first quarter profits to the pound's rally. -- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
